state:
NimbleBank Overdraft Courtesy Policy:
- First overdraft in a rolling 12-month period: fee automatically waived if the account is brought back to a positive balance within 24 hours.
- Overdrafts caused by a pending merchant hold that is later reversed (for example, a hotel or rental car deposit) are never charged a fee, regardless of timing or overdraft history.
- Customers enrolled in Overdraft Protection (linked savings transfer) are not eligible for courtesy waivers, since the transfer should prevent the overdraft in the first place; a fee appearing in that case indicates a system error requiring manual review, not a standard waiver.

Case notes, account ending 2290: Overdrew by $42 on September 5 due to a $200 hotel deposit hold that was released back on September 7 once checkout was confirmed by the hotel. Balance returned to positive on September 6, within 24 hours of the overdraft. Account is not enrolled in Overdraft Protection. This is the account's first overdraft in the past 14 months, per the account history on file.

Customer's message: "Hey, I noticed a $35 overdraft fee from September 5th. I'm pretty sure this was from a hotel hold, not an actual purchase, since the charge disappeared a couple days later when I checked out. Can you take a look? I'm not in a huge hurry, I just don't want to forget about this and let it slide past whatever window you have for disputing it. Also, totally separate question while I have you -- do you know if NimbleBank ever plans to support Zelle for business accounts, or is that still just personal accounts only?"

Support agent's internal note: Verified hotel hold matches the dates the customer describes; merchant category code confirms lodging deposit, consistent with a reversible hold rather than a completed purchase. Account has otherwise been in good standing for the full 6 years it has been open, with autopay enabled on the linked credit card for recurring bills. No prior contact from this customer regarding fees of any kind in that time.

Follow-up note added by a second reviewer: Cross-checked against the July and August statements as well; no other overdrafts or holds of this size appear in that period, consistent with the customer's description of this being an isolated event tied specifically to travel. Reviewer recommends closing this as a standard courtesy waiver rather than escalating to the fraud or disputes team, since none of the manual-review triggers in the Overdraft Protection clause apply here.

PulseFit Refund Policy:
- Annual plans: refundable in full within 14 days of purchase, no questions asked.
- Annual plans after 14 days: refundable on a prorated basis only if the member can show the app was unusable due to a verified bug for 7 or more consecutive days.
- Monthly plans: non-refundable after 3 days, no exceptions.
- Personal training add-on packages: always non-refundable once the first session in the package has been completed, regardless of how many sessions remain unused.

Ticket: Member Dana K., annual plan purchased 47 days ago. Reports the workout-sync feature was completely broken from August 1-11 (11 consecutive days), confirmed in PulseFit's own status page incident log INC-2231. Dana also purchased a 5-session personal training add-on 30 days ago and has completed 1 session so far.

Dana's message: "Hi, I want to request a refund. The app's sync feature was broken for what looks like almost two weeks in August based on your own status page, which made the annual plan pretty useless to me during that stretch, so I'd like some money back for that. Separately, I also want to cancel the remaining 4 personal training sessions I haven't used yet and get those refunded too, since my schedule changed. No huge rush on either, just want to get both sorted this month."

Support agent's internal note, added after pulling the account history: Dana has been a member for just over a year with no prior refund requests of any kind. The status page incident log for INC-2231 confirms sync was down for all users from August 1 00:00 to August 11 19:40, matching Dana's description almost exactly. Training package invoice shows session 1 completed on day 17 of the 30-day-old package, with sessions 2 through 5 still marked 'unused' in the scheduling system as of today. Billing team's standard response template for verified multi-day outages includes a suggested proration formula: refund percentage equals affected days divided by 30, applied to the monthly-equivalent portion of the annual fee, though the exact dollar figure still needs a manager's sign-off before it's quoted to the member. Separately, the training package terms Dana agreed to at purchase explicitly list the no-refund-after-first-session rule in bold text, which the account specialist flagged as worth quoting back verbatim in the reply so there's no ambiguity about why that half of the request can't be honored, even though the specialist personally sympathizes with the scheduling-change reason Dana gave.
